formulas.name: Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)
formulas.formula: CAC = Total Sales & Marketing Spend / Number of New Customers Acquired

worked_example.insight: The question: does each customer eventually generate more than ₹2,000 in profit? If yes, model works. If no, buying growth at a loss.
worked_example.problem: Zomato spends ₹800 crore on S&M, acquires 40 lakh new customers.

formulas.name: Customer Lifetime Value (CLTV)

variables.ARPU: Average Revenue Per User per period
variables.CLTV: Total profit a customer generates over entire relationship
variables.Churn Rate: % of customers who stop using the product per period

benchmarks.1x_to_3x: Marginal. Need to reduce CAC or improve retention/margins.
benchmarks.above_3x: Healthy unit economics. Business model works.
benchmarks.below_1x: Broken. Every new customer destroys value.

formulas.sensitivity: If churn increases from 8% to 12%, CLTV drops to ₹5,833 and ratio falls to 2.9x — borderline. Churn is the silent killer of unit economics.

worked_example.problem: Zomato: 8 orders/month × ₹350 AOV = ₹2,800 ARPU. Gross margin 25%. Monthly churn 8%.

worked_example.insight: Each passenger contributes ₹2,300 toward fixed costs. IndiGo's genius: fixed costs per seat among lowest in world (single aircraft type A320, high seat density, fast turnaround).

formulas.name: Operating Leverage (DOL)
formulas.formula: DOL = % Change in Operating Profit / % Change in Revenue
formulas.flip_side: Works in reverse: if revenue falls 20%, profit could fall 40%. Why high-operating-leverage businesses (airlines, hotels, steel, software) are more volatile and often have higher betas.

worked_example.insight: 20% revenue increase → 40% profit increase. Fixed cost base doesn't grow, so incremental revenue flows to profit.
worked_example.problem: Zoho: Y1 Revenue ₹5,000cr, Op Profit ₹1,500cr. Y2 Revenue ₹6,000cr (+20%), Op Profit ₹2,100cr (+40%).

formulas.name: Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)
formulas.formula: CAC = Total Sales & Marketing Spend / Number of New Customers Acquired

variables.meaning: Aggregate expenditure on advertising, promotions, sales team, and customer acquisition activities over a period
Count of unique new customers gained during the same period

formulas.plain_english: CAC tells you how much you must spend in sales and marketing to bring in one new customer. The lower the CAC, the more efficient your customer acquisition. For a unit economics model to be healthy, CAC must be significantly lower than the profit each customer eventually generates (CLTV).

worked_example.problem: Zomato spends ₹800 crore on S&M, acquires 40 lakh new customers.
worked_example.insight: The question: does each customer eventually generate more than ₹2,000 in profit? If yes, model works. If no, buying growth at a loss.

formulas.name: Customer Lifetime Value (CLTV)

variables.meaning: Average Revenue Per User per period (typically monthly or annual)
(Revenue - COGS) / Revenue; expressed as a decimal (e.g., 0.25 for 25%)
Fraction of customers who stop using the product per period (e.g., 0.08 for 8% monthly churn)
Total discounted profit a customer generates over their entire relationship with the company

formulas.plain_english: CLTV quantifies the total lifetime profit from one customer. It reflects how much gross profit the customer generates each period, adjusted for how long they stay (inverse of churn). A healthy unit economics model requires CLTV to be at least 3× CAC; anything below 1× CAC means customer acquisition is destroying value.

benchmarks.1x_to_3x: Marginal. Need to reduce CAC or improve retention/margins.
benchmarks.above_3x: Healthy unit economics. Business model works.
benchmarks.below_1x: Broken. Every new customer destroys value.

formulas.sensitivity: If churn increases from 8% to 12%, CLTV drops to ₹5,833 and ratio falls to 2.9x — borderline. Churn is the silent killer of unit economics.

worked_example.problem: Zomato: 8 orders/month × ₹350 AOV = ₹2,800 ARPU. Gross margin 25%. Monthly churn 8%.
worked_example.insight: CLTV/CAC = 4.375x → Healthy (>3x benchmark). Each customer eventually generates 4.4× the cost to acquire them.

formulas.name: Contribution Margin

variables.meaning: Total sales or price per unit
Costs that change directly with production or sales volume (e.g., raw materials, direct labour, packaging)

formulas.plain_english: Contribution margin shows how much profit each sale generates after paying the direct costs to produce or deliver it. It represents the pool of money available to cover fixed costs (rent, salaries, depreciation) and fund profit. A negative contribution margin means the business loses money on every additional sale — a critical red flag.
formulas.why_it_matters: How much each sale contributes toward covering fixed costs and generating profit. If negative, every additional sale makes the company poorer.

worked_example.problem: IndiGo Airlines: ticket ₹5,500. Variable costs: fuel ₹2,200, airport ₹600, food ₹100, other ₹300 = ₹3,200.
worked_example.insight: Each passenger contributes ₹2,300 toward fixed costs. IndiGo's genius: fixed costs per seat among lowest in world (single aircraft type A320, high seat density, fast turnaround).

formulas.name: Operating Leverage (DOL)
formulas.formula: DOL = % Change in Operating Profit / % Change in Revenue

variables.meaning: Percentage increase or decrease in operating profit (EBIT) from one period to the next
Percentage increase or decrease in total revenue from one period to the next
Degree of Operating Leverage; a multiplier showing how sensitive operating profit is to revenue changes

formulas.plain_english: Operating leverage measures how much operating profit moves when revenue moves. A DOL of 2.0× means a 1% change in revenue produces a 2% change in profit. High operating leverage (DOL > 2) amplifies upside but also downside; it reflects a business with high fixed costs and low variable costs, common in airlines, hotels, software, and steel.
computation: Calculate operating profit (EBIT) for Year 1 and Year 2.
Find % change in revenue: [(Revenue Y2 - Revenue Y1) / Revenue Y1] × 100
Find % change in EBIT: [(EBIT Y2 - EBIT Y1) / EBIT Y1] × 100
Divide % change in EBIT by % change in revenue to get DOL.
formulas.flip_side: Works in reverse: if revenue falls 20%, profit could fall 40%. Why high-operating-leverage businesses (airlines, hotels, steel, software) are more volatile and often have higher betas.

worked_example.problem: Zoho: Y1 Revenue ₹5,000cr, Op Profit ₹1,500cr. Y2 Revenue ₹6,000cr (+20%), Op Profit ₹2,100cr (+40%).
worked_example.insight: 20% revenue increase → 40% profit increase. Fixed cost base doesn't grow, so incremental revenue flows to profit. This leverage is powerful in good times but risks rapid margin compression if revenue contracts.
